creator: Sabine Hossenfelder
title: Some UAPs Might Be Warp Drives, Physicists Say
full_text:
An astrophysicist has claimed that some
unidentified anomalous phenomena that
were observed in recent years in the
United States might be warp drives. And
he's written a paper about it. And his
name is Avi Loeb.
Well, let's have a look. In October
2023,
six federal agents in the western United
States saw an orange glowing orb appear,
release clusters of smaller red orbs,
and vanish. We have no videos of the
incident, but we have this
reconstruction from the witness reports.
It's happened repeatedly over two
evenings. According to the Pentagon
report, there were two different teams
of agents which observed the same thing.
What they called an orange mother orb
appeared for 1 or 2 seconds, released
between two and four smaller red orbs,
and then disappeared. This pattern
repeated several times over a period of
hours. The red objects moved silently,
appeared to change altitude, and one
reportedly remained stationary above a
ridge for several hours. The Pentagon
has called the case orbs launching orbs
and launched an investigation, but they
couldn't come up with any plausible
explanation. Drones, they said, were
unlikely because they can't remain
airborne for that long, at least none
that could do this were known in 2023.
Weather conditions did not favor ball
lightning or other unusual atmospheric
effects, and they couldn't explain it
with any of their own technologies,
either, like infrared weapons which they
tested in the area at the time. So, they
don't know what it is. The Harvard
astrophysicist Avi Loeb has now taken an
interest in the case and says that the
objects could be explained by tiny
space-time bubbles on the scale of
several micrometers.
>> The anomalous orbs reported by the
Pentagon indeed move at slow speeds and
could be explained by tiny space-time
bubbles on the scale of several
micrometers.
>> And he has written a paper about this
with a colleague that appeared as a
preprint on the archive. So, it hasn't
been peer-reviewed. In the paper, they
look at what it would look like if a
warp drive bubble were to move through
Earth's atmosphere. A warp drive for a
physicist is a type of space-time
deformation in Einstein's theory of
general relativity. The idea is that an
object is propelled forward by
contracting space-time before it and
expanding it behind it. This could, in
principle, allow the object to move
faster than the speed of light because
that barrier exists only for objects
moving in space-time. It doesn't extend
to the deformation of space-time itself.
In the paper now, the astrophysicists
calculate what happens if such a warp
drive bubble of size between 25 and 100
m diameter travels through the
atmosphere at a significant fraction of
the speed of light. What happens is not
very mysterious. It creates a shock
wave. The air heats up and turns into an
extremely hot plasma, which emits x-rays
and gamma rays, which we can't see. But,
much of this high-energy radiation is
absorbed further down in the atmosphere,
where it's partly converted into visible
and ultraviolet light. An observer on
the ground would therefore see an
intense atmospheric glow below the
bubble's path, and you'd see that
basically all across the United States.
To make a long story short, the advanced
extraterrestrial technology is doing an
excellent impression of a meteor, which,
well, is not what the agent saw.
However, the observed brightness of the
warp drive falls very rapidly as the
warp bubble becomes smaller. If the
bubble is only a few micrometers across
and moves at a few times the speed of
sound, then Loeb and his colleague argue
the warp drive could produce the sort of
modest glow reported by the agents.
Therefore, Avi Loeb says, well, if it's
a warp bubble, then it's a very small
one that doesn't move very fast. What
are we to make of this? This gets an
eight out of 10 on the meter. I
think that it's fine to ask, well, if
these things existed, what did they look
like traveling through the atmosphere?
The problem is that these observable
signatures in the atmosphere depend
pretty much only on the size and speed
of the object and not on just what its
propulsion system is. The other problem
with the paper is that it's completely
uncritical about the idea of warp drives
to begin with. You see all this talk
about warping space-time still does let
you violate momentum conservation. If
you want to accelerate an object in one
direction, you still have to throw
something out into the other direction.
And if you want your object to move
faster than light, then you have to
throw out something with negative
energy, which doesn't make it any
easier. You see, the warp bubble idea
isn't doing any work. It's superfluous
decoration for people who are
intimidated by general relativity. You
still need a propulsion system for the
thing to accelerate. That said, it's an
unfortunate truth that agent education
make you narrow-minded. So, I think one
has to give credit to Avi Loeb that he's
trying to avoid this. However, several
people have independently told me that
the US military has an interest in the
physics of warp drives and hyper drives,
and I think physicists have not been
entirely honest in pointing out the
shortcomings of their theories about
this. Good thing you have me to do this.
This video does not have a sponsor,
which means I paid to bring it to you.
If you want to see more of my science
news, please consider supporting me
either on Patreon or right here on
YouTube. And if you already support me,
thank you so much. A big thank you
especially to those of you in our
Patreon tier four and higher. This
channel would not be possible without
your help. Thanks for watching. See you
tomorrow.

notes.note: AARO's analysis did not rule out infrared tech. The report cites U.S. military infrared countermeasure flares, confirmed by flight logs as deployed in the area, as the leading explanation for ~60% of reported activity, leaving only up to ~40% unexplained.

sources.quote: Historical flight logs confirm that U.S. military aircraft operating in the area were equipped with, and actively deployed, infrared countermeasure flares as a component of a standard exercise.
sources.explanation: This confirms that military infrared technology was present and active in the area during the incident.

sources.quote: AARO assesses that the characteristics described in the agents’ narrative account align with those of certain U.S. military technologies.
sources.explanation: This supports the claim that AARO did not rule out U.S. technology and actually found similarities.

sources.quote: The phenomena’s position relative to the observers, perceived direction of travel, and time of observation strongly align with historical radar and ADS-B data, suggesting that approximately 60 percent of the reported activity is plausibly attributable to military aircraft.
sources.explanation: This directly supports the claim that roughly 60% of the activity was explained by military activity (flares).

sources.quote: Approximately 40 percent of the reported phenomena lack a plausible explanation after first stage analysis and thus remain unresolved.
sources.explanation: This supports the claim that up to 40% remains unexplained.

sources.quote: AARO has admitted that 40 per cent of the reported activity remains unexplained.

notes.opus_reason: Sabine is summarising the Pentagon report in her own voice, not quoting someone she disputes: she says the Pentagon 'couldn't come up with any plausible explanation', that 'they couldn't explain it with any of their own technologies, either, like infrared weapons which they tested in the area at the time', and 'so, they don't know what it is'. I read the actual AARO memorandum (Western U.S. Event 'Orbs Launching Orbs', 05 June 2026, signed by AARO director Jon T. Kosloski) and every quote the note was accepted on appears in it word for word. The memo rates 'Military Aircraft Dispensing Flares' as partially plausible, says flight logs confirm U.S. military aircraft in the area actively deployed infrared countermeasure flares during a standard exercise, that the reported shape and behaviour align with known characteristics of certain military infrared flares, and that radar and ADS-B data suggest approximately 60 percent of the reported activity is plausibly attributable to military aircraft, with about 40 percent left unresolved. So the specific sentence the note is attached to is wrong: the Pentagon did explain most of the sightings with its own technology, and the only hypothesis it actually ruled out was aircraft exhaust. This matters to the video's point, because the whole setup is that the case is a complete mystery that invites Avi Loeb's warp-drive paper. The note does leave out that the agents themselves said the objects did not look like flares and that the case as a whole is officially still unresolved, but it never claims otherwise, and a physicist who is this careful about what reports actually say will most likely welcome a correction that points back at the mundane explanation in the primary document.
